sabbath-day
The Seventh-Day Sabbath

The command names the day as belonging to the LORD. Read its designation rather than substituting a familiar worship custom. The question concerns the day the passage actually calls Sabbath, not a vote about later practice.
Identify the Sabbath from the command’s own wording.
wisdom-soul
Wisdom and the Character of the Soul

The verse concerns the kind of person receiving wisdom, rather than a location or a title of office. A malicious character is the contrast being tested. Learning the wording should also direct attention to the moral condition described.
Connect the pursuit of wisdom with the character the passage describes.
hear-first
Hear Before Answering

The instruction orders listening before an answer. This makes understanding the cause a prerequisite to responding. In practice, an answer given before hearing can address an imagined case instead of the one actually presented; the verse directs the opposite sequence.
Explain why hearing the cause must precede the reply.
unleavened-days
The Days of Unleavened Bread

This is an appointed observance with a stated duration and a particular food instruction. Keep the period named in the command distinct from other feasts and assemblies. Remembering its duration helps identify the observance without treating all feast instructions as interchangeable.
Distinguish this feast’s stated duration and observance.
honor-parents
Honouring Father and Mother

The command names both parents. Its wording directs attention to a relationship and an obligation, rather than a person’s social position. Do not replace either named parent with another authority when identifying whom this command specifically tells the hearer to honour.
Recognize both parents as the recipients of the stated duty.
guard-heart
Guarding the Heart

The instruction describes a continuing responsibility, expressed as keeping the heart with diligence. Its stated reason concerns the issues of life proceeding from it. The image therefore teaches watchfulness over the inner source of conduct, rather than attention to appearances alone.
Connect guarding the heart with the reason Proverbs supplies.
trust-lord
Trusting the LORD

The verse sets two objects of reliance in contrast: the LORD and one’s own understanding. The lesson is about where trust rests, rather than a claim that understanding itself is the enemy. Preserve the contrast the proverb actually makes.
Distinguish trust in the LORD from reliance on one’s own understanding.
hope-deferred
Hope and Fulfilled Desire

The proverb contrasts delay with fulfilment. Reading both sides prevents the first phrase from becoming an isolated claim about every kind of suffering. The question asks for the experience the text names as making the heart sick, within that contrast.
Explain the proverb’s contrast between deferred hope and fulfilled desire.
receive-commandments
Wisdom Receives Commandments

The saying identifies wisdom through a response to instruction: receiving commandments. It does not define the wise person merely by reputation, wealth or verbal ability. The question asks what is received, while the teaching connects wisdom with receptiveness to direction.
Recognize receiving commandments as the response associated with wisdom.
enemy-falls
When an Enemy Stumbles

The warning concerns the observer’s response when an enemy experiences misfortune. Hostility does not make delight in that fall the instructed response. Keep this moral restraint distinct from questions about lawful judgment or how the enemy’s difficulty came about.
Distinguish an enemy’s misfortune from permission to rejoice in it.
moses-brother
Aaron and Moses

The LORD’s question identifies Aaron by both a family relationship and a Levitical description. The lesson is careful identification: distinguish the person explicitly named as Moses’ brother from other leaders who appear in Israel’s story or assist Moses at other times.
Identify Aaron through the relationship explicitly stated in Exodus.
jonah-days
Jonah in the Fish

The time statement includes both days and nights. Preserve the full description instead of replacing it with a general expression such as a short stay. The question asks about Jonah’s narrated experience, without requiring an added timetable beyond this passage.
Read the account’s complete description of Jonah’s time in the fish.
creation-rest
The Day of Creation Rest

The creation narrative specifies which day is associated with God’s rest. A later custom cannot change that identification within Genesis. First observe the day named by the text; questions about later practice require their own passages and cannot supply a different answer here.
Separate Genesis’ stated day from assumptions about later practice.
spirit-sword
The Sword of the Spirit

The verse gives an identification within the armor imagery: the sword is the word of God. Treat that explanatory phrase as decisive. Other equipment names belong to the imagery, but they are not substitutes for what this sentence identifies as the sword.
Identify the sword from the passage’s explanatory phrase.
wise-count
Gifts Do Not Establish a Visitor Count

The narrative gives types of gifts without supplying a count of the visitors. A familiar picture can join those two details into an assumption, but the inference is not a stated number. Careful reading distinguishes something recorded from something left unspecified.
Distinguish the number of gifts from an unstated number of visitors.
wise-house
Read the Wise Men’s Visit Carefully

A remembered scene can combine details from separate accounts or moments. This question asks for the location Matthew names for this visit. Observe that location before combining it with other birth narratives; a combined illustration cannot replace the wording being tested.
Identify this visit’s setting from Matthew’s own description.
david-stones
What David Chose Before the Battle

The count belongs to David’s preparation, not simply to the stone used in the encounter. Keep selection and later use as distinct actions. This small narrative distinction illustrates why knowing an outcome does not establish every detail of the preparation.
Distinguish the stones selected from the stone later used.
antioch-name
The Disciples at Antioch

The sentence attaches the naming to a particular place. The lesson is to retain the account’s geographical identification rather than choose a city merely because it is prominent elsewhere. A historically familiar name still needs the location the passage supplies.
Locate the naming of the disciples in the cited account.
vengeance
Leave Repayment to the Lord

The instruction addresses the reader’s conduct toward retaliation and then attributes repayment to the Lord. Naming the speaker of the repayment statement preserves that distinction. It must not be turned into authorization for a reader to claim the same unrestricted right personally.
Distinguish the instruction against self-vengeance from the Lord’s repayment.
city-descends
John’s Description of the Holy City

Observe both the city’s name and the movement John describes. The question tests that vision’s explicit description, not an unprovided date or complete sequence of future events. Keeping observation separate from a proposed timetable makes later comparison more responsible.
Identify the city and the direction described in John’s vision.
raphael
Raphael Identifies Himself

This traditional KJV Apocrypha passage identifies its speaker directly. Use that self-identification rather than another familiar angelic name. The question does not require inventing an additional rank, mission or doctrine beyond what the cited statement itself supplies.
Recognize the speaker through the passage’s self-identification.
learned-leisure
Opportunity for Learned Wisdom

The saying connects learning with an opportunity for leisure and reduced business. Read it as the relationship this wisdom passage describes, rather than a claim that a title or possession automatically creates wisdom. The question asks about opportunity, not a guarantee for every individual.
Explain the opportunity connected with learned wisdom in the passage.
esdras-comparison
Read the Named Comparison

The passage places two names in a comparison of an end and a beginning. Keep those named roles in their stated order. This wording does not supply a modern population identification, so that additional claim must not be imported as the answer.
Preserve the named end-and-beginning comparison without adding modern identities.
law-prophets-psalms
Yeshua and the Scriptural Witness

Yeshua identifies bodies of Scripture containing things concerning himself. The teaching encourages reading those writings in relation to his explanation. It does not make familiarity with one isolated verse a substitute for attending to the scriptural divisions he actually names.
Recognize the three scriptural divisions named in Yeshua’s explanation.
salem-meaning
The Meaning of Salem

The passage interprets titles and distinguishes their meanings. Follow the phrase attached to King of Salem rather than transferring the adjacent interpretation of righteousness to it. Keeping the two explanations separate is necessary before drawing a larger comparison from the passage.
Distinguish the meanings assigned to the two royal titles.
weightier-matters
Judgment, Mercy and Faith

The rebuke identifies neglected moral responsibilities while also speaking about the other observance. Do not turn a statement about weightier matters into permission to discard everything else. The lesson is to preserve both the named priorities and the qualification in the saying.
Recognize the named weightier matters without deleting the accompanying qualification.
measure-number-weight
Measure, Number and Weight

The saying presents an ordered description using three terms together. Retaining all three prevents a partial recollection from replacing the full expression. This traditional KJV Apocrypha question concerns the text’s description of ordering, not a speculative numerical system built from it.
Recognize the complete three-part description of ordering.
apollos-origin
Apollos’ Origin and Arrival

A person’s birthplace and the city where the narrative later places him are different facts. The account supplies both kinds of identification. Answer the geographical relationship actually asked, rather than letting the most recently mentioned place stand for every part of his history.
Distinguish Apollos’ birthplace from the location of his arrival.
lydia-city
Lydia’s City and the Narrative Setting

The city associated with Lydia must not be confused with the setting in which the encounter is narrated. Her description also identifies her trade. Read the relationship between person and place carefully instead of choosing the city most familiar from the wider account.
Distinguish Lydia’s city identification from the encounter’s setting.
sychar
Sychar and Jacob’s Gift

John joins a city name with a nearby parcel associated with Jacob and Joseph. These details locate the scene rather than provide interchangeable names for one person. Retaining the geographical description supports understanding the setting of the following encounter.
Locate the named Samaritan city within John’s description.
land-animals
Both Land-Animal Criteria Matter

The criteria are joined requirements, not competing alternatives. Identifying one feature without the other does not reproduce the rule being tested. This is a lesson in reading a command’s conditions together before applying its classification to a particular animal.
Apply both stated criteria rather than treating either one as sufficient.
water-creatures
Fins and Scales

The permitted description joins two characteristics and applies them to creatures in the waters. Keep those requirements together. A familiar association with water alone does not answer the question about the features the law actually names for this category.
Identify the two features named for permitted water creatures.
six-days
Labour and Sabbath Rest

The labor instruction belongs beside the following Sabbath instruction. Reading the sequence distinguishes the days assigned for work from the day identified for rest. Do not substitute the entire seven-day sequence for the number of labor days the question asks about.
Distinguish the stated labor period from the following Sabbath day.
love-commandments
Love Expressed in Keeping Commandments

The saying connects the disciples’ love for Yeshua with a concrete response to his commandments. It asks for more than an affectionate label. Preserve the action named in the instruction rather than substituting a different religious activity as its explicit completion.
Recognize commandment-keeping as the response named in the saying about love.
hands-complaint
Identify the Handwashing Dispute

Before applying a conclusion, identify the accusation that begins the discussion. Here the issue named is a handwashing practice associated with the elders’ tradition. Starting with that stated dispute prevents a different question about food or conduct from silently replacing it.
Identify the dispute’s stated subject before drawing a broader application.
hands-conclusion
What the Passage Says Defiles

The concluding statement contrasts the evils described as proceeding from the heart with eating using unwashed hands. Retain that particular contrast. It does not name every possible food, so the sentence should not be made to answer a different classification question without further evidence.
Preserve the passage’s stated contrast without broadening its scope.
establish-law
Paul Rejects Making the Law Void

Paul frames a question about faith and the law, then rejects the proposed conclusion. Read his reply rather than assume what faith must mean for the law. The lesson is careful argument reading: an objection raised in a letter is not automatically the writer’s teaching.
Distinguish Paul’s rejected proposal from his stated answer about the law.
doers-word
Hear the Word and Act

The instruction contrasts hearing with doing, not careful listening with careless listening alone. Receiving words without acting is the problem being addressed. The accompanying comparison develops that difference, so the required response must include conduct rather than mere exposure to instruction.
Explain the difference between hearing the word and acting on it.
command-tradition
Commandment and Human Tradition

The reply evaluates a tradition by whether it transgresses God’s commandment. The following parental-duty example keeps the issue concrete. Do not assume that a familiar religious practice is exempt from comparison with the command simply because it is presented as devotion.
Evaluate the stated tradition by its relationship to the commandment.
grace-sin
Grace Is Not Permission to Sin

The letter raises the possibility of sin under grace and immediately rejects it. Separate the question being answered from Paul’s own response. The following discussion of obedience and service should not be replaced by a slogan that grants the permission he denies.
Distinguish grace from the permission to sin that Paul explicitly rejects.
keeping-commandments
Read Paul’s Stated Contrast

Paul’s discussion names circumcision and uncircumcision before identifying keeping God’s commandments. Read the complete contrast instead of omitting its final clause. This wording can be identified directly without claiming that one sentence resolves every question about the passage’s applications.
Identify the positive emphasis in Paul’s stated contrast.
teach-children
Teaching the Words in Daily Life

The instruction places teaching within recurring household and daily activities. It is not limited to an isolated formal occasion. Attend to both the named learners and the repeated settings, so that knowing whom to teach also leads to understanding the described pattern of instruction.
Explain how teaching children is woven into the daily settings named.
bke-melchizedek-gifts
Melchizedek’s Provisions

The account identifies Melchizedek as both king and priest while describing what he brings. Keep the actor, his titles and the provisions distinct. The question asks about a narrated action, not an unprovided explanation of every later use of Melchizedek’s priesthood.
Identify the action while preserving the account’s named actor and titles.
bke-joseph-age
Joseph Before Pharaoh

The age is attached to Joseph standing before Pharaoh and then going through Egypt. It belongs to this point in the narrative, not to his earlier experiences with his brothers. A remembered age must be connected to the correct event.
Locate Joseph’s stated age at the audience with Pharaoh.
bke-moses-hands
Support in the Battle with Amalek

The verse describes several coordinated actions: providing a stone, Moses sitting, and Aaron and Hur supporting his hands until sunset. This separates those assisting Moses from Joshua’s role in the battle, showing why the named helpers matter to the scene.
Distinguish the supporters of Moses’ hands from the battle’s other participants.
bke-oshea-name
The Name Given to Oshea

The naming statement occurs in the list of men Moses sends to spy out the land. Keep the person being renamed distinct from other men in that list. The KJV form Jehoshua is the wording being tested in this passage.
Identify the name given in this particular naming statement.
bke-jordan-season
The River at Harvest

The account connects the priests’ arrival at the water with a parenthetical description of the river’s seasonal overflow. That detail helps establish the crossing’s setting. The question asks about the season named, not a guessed date or a different river event.
Use the narrative’s seasonal detail to understand the crossing’s setting.
bke-ruth-husband
Ruth and Boaz

The verse narrates marriage, conception and the birth of a son. Identify the husband in that stated sequence rather than transferring an earlier family relationship into the later scene. Careful attention to sequence distinguishes this marriage from Ruth’s preceding history.
Distinguish this marriage from Ruth’s earlier family relationships.
bke-elijah-water
The First Pouring at Carmel

The instruction joins the ordered wood and prepared sacrifice with pouring water. The requested number belongs to this first instruction. Later repetitions of an action must be counted separately instead of being substituted for the number initially requested.
Distinguish the initial instruction from later repetitions of pouring.
bke-nehemiah-office
Prayer and a Royal Office

Nehemiah’s prayer asks for mercy in the sight of the man before identifying his position as the king’s cupbearer. Read that office in its immediate prayer setting. A different royal title may sound plausible but does not match the identity supplied here.
Connect Nehemiah’s named office with the setting of his prayer.
bke-enemy-burden
Help Despite Hostility

The instruction explicitly names an owner who hates the observer and an animal in difficulty. The stated response is help rather than withholding assistance. The owner’s hostility is therefore part of the moral challenge, not an exception cancelling the duty.
Apply the stated duty even when the owner is hostile.
bke-neighbor-love
Neighbour-Love Without Vengeance

The command about love appears beside prohibitions on vengeance and grudges. Read those directions together: the comparison with oneself belongs to instructions about how a neighbour is treated. It is not an excuse to preserve resentment while claiming the language of love.
Connect neighbour-love with the surrounding restraint on vengeance and grudges.
bke-impartial-court
Justice Without Favouritism

The verse names favoritism toward both poverty and power as dangers to judgment. Righteous judgment is the positive direction. Sympathy or social standing must not replace the standard the verse gives for deciding a neighbour’s case.
Distinguish righteous judgment from partiality toward either social position.
bke-trumpets-date
A Memorial and Holy Convocation

The date belongs to an instruction naming rest, a memorial of blowing trumpets and a holy convocation. Keep this observance distinct from other dates in the seventh month. Learning the date should locate the instruction, not collapse separate appointed times into one.
Identify this appointed time by its date and named observances.
bke-annual-appearances
The Three Named Appearances

The instruction names three feasts and the place the LORD chooses, then says not to appear empty. Preserve the actual list rather than assume every feast is one of these appearances. The number alone does not explain which occasions the command identifies.
Distinguish the three named appearances from other observances.
bke-king-law-copy
The King Receives the Law

The king’s accession is followed by an instruction to write a copy from the law before the Levitical priests. This places his action in relation to an existing authoritative text. It does not describe a king inventing commandments to fit his preferences.
Recognize the king as a recipient and copier of the existing law.
bke-forgotten-sheaf
Provision Left in the Harvest

The command concerns a sheaf already forgotten in the field and forbids returning to fetch it. It names beneficiaries and connects the instruction with blessing in the worker’s labours. Notice both the circumstance that triggers the rule and whom it serves.
Identify the circumstance and beneficiaries of the forgotten-sheaf instruction.
bke-later-passover
A Specified Passover Provision

The cited passages join particular eligibility circumstances with a later date and prescribed foods. This is a provision with stated conditions, not permission to choose any convenient day. Reading the condition before the date keeps the exception within the law’s own scope.
Keep the later observance connected to its stated conditions.
bke-reconcile-first
Reconciliation Before Returning

The instruction establishes an order: leave the gift, seek reconciliation, and then return to offer. That sequence prevents the offering from being treated as a substitute for addressing the relational wrong. The lesson concerns the action required before proceeding with worship.
Explain the priority of reconciliation in the stated sequence.
bke-rock-hearer
Hearing That Becomes Action

The builder comparison describes a person who hears the sayings and does them. Both responses belong to the comparison. Do not replace that paired description with hearing alone, even when the words have been received attentively or remembered accurately.
Identify both responses included in the wise-builder comparison.
bke-mercy-hosea
Mercy and the Guiltless

Yeshua applies the mercy statement to the condemnation of people he calls guiltless. Compare the saying with its named prophetic connection while preserving this immediate accusation setting. A shared phrase does not, by itself, rewrite every instruction about sacrifice.
Relate the mercy statement to its immediate use against wrongful condemnation.
bke-sabbath-for-man
The Sabbath and Its Stated Relationship

The saying gives the direction of a relationship between humanity and the Sabbath. Preserve that direction when explaining it. This observation is distinct from settling every later debate about particular Sabbath applications, which would require examining the relevant contexts and instructions separately.
Explain the relationship in the order the saying actually states.
bke-neighbor-mercy
Mercy That Identifies a Neighbour

The reply identifies the one who showed mercy, and Yeshua follows it with an instruction to act likewise. The teaching therefore moves from identifying the neighbourly action to doing it. It does not end at naming the person in the story.
Connect the identified act of mercy with the instruction to act likewise.
bke-chief-serves
Greatness Expressed in Service

Yeshua contrasts the disciples’ conduct with the exercise of lordship described around them. The chief is directed to serve. This makes greatness a responsibility toward others rather than permission to imitate the conduct being contrasted with their calling.
Explain the service required of the one who is chief.
bke-footwashing-example
The Master’s Example

The argument identifies the speaker as Lord and Master before drawing a responsibility for the disciples from his own action. Attend to that movement from example to instruction. The question tests the action named rather than requiring a denominational account of the practice.
Connect the Master’s action with the stated responsibility toward one another.
bke-peter-joel
Peter Names His Prophetic Source

Peter introduces the following explanation by naming a prophet. Start with that explicit source identification rather than selecting a different prophet because of a familiar theme. The citation then needs to be read in its own context before building additional prophetic conclusions.
Identify the named prophetic source before extending the interpretation.
bke-david-tabernacle
David’s Fallen Tent and Restoration

The comparison preserves the image of a fallen structure being raised and repaired. Acts uses that prophetic language in a council discussion. Identifying the shared restoration image is a first step; it does not establish an entire sequence or date for the prophecy.
Identify the shared restoration image without adding a timetable.
bke-abraham-counted
Paul Appeals to Abraham’s Scripture

Paul introduces the statement by asking what Scripture says. His argument therefore points the reader back to a written account rather than an assumed slogan. Compare the cited wording carefully without claiming that identifying the shared statement resolves every wider faith-and-works question.
Recognize the scriptural statement Paul uses in his argument about Abraham.
bke-enemy-provision
Responding to an Enemy’s Need

The instructions specify food for hunger and drink for thirst. Those immediate actions remain clear even when readers debate the coals image. Distinguish the observable conduct commanded from an additional explanation of its effect on the enemy.
Identify the concrete response commanded for an enemy’s immediate needs.
bke-rock-comparison
The Wilderness Rock in Paul’s Account

Exodus narrates provision of water, while Paul describes spiritual drink and identifies the Rock as Christ. Keep the historical provision and Paul’s stated identification distinct within the comparison. The question reports his words without inventing a mechanism for the image.
Distinguish the wilderness provision from Paul’s explicit identification of the Rock.
bke-law-hearts
The Covenant’s Inward Law

The covenant wording speaks of laws in mind and heart alongside the relationship of God and people. Compare that inward location in both passages. The shared statement should be retained without pretending that it alone answers every question about covenant recipients or applications.
Recognize the inward location of the law in the compared covenant passages.
bke-no-deceit
Truthfulness in the Prophetic Comparison

The comparison concerns what is absent from the subject’s mouth. Different English terms can express the observed connection, so follow the descriptions rather than demand identical spelling. This is a textual comparison, not permission to invent additional details about either passage’s setting.
Recognize the shared denial of falsehood in the compared descriptions.
bke-weak-received
Reception Without Doubtful Disputes

The instruction concerns receiving a person and qualifies how that reception is approached. Keep that positive action and qualification together. A reader should not turn this one sentence into a complete answer to every disputed practice addressed elsewhere in the chapter.
Explain the required reception while retaining its stated qualification.
bke-corban-meaning
A Gift and a Neglected Parent

The gloss identifies the term as a gift, but the argument concerns withholding benefit from parents. A religious label is therefore not the same as approval of the conduct described. Separate what the word means from how the passage evaluates its use.
Distinguish the term’s meaning from approval of withholding parental support.
bke-law-reveals-coveting
What the Command Reveals

Paul first rejects identifying the law itself with sin, then uses the command against coveting to explain knowledge of sin. Preserve that order. His negative answer to the first question and his positive example serve different parts of the argument.
Explain the command’s role without confusing the law itself with sin.
bke-liberty-service
Liberty Directed Toward Love

Paul gives a warning and a positive direction in the same instruction. Liberty is not to become an occasion to the flesh; love is expressed in serving one another. Retaining both clauses avoids replacing the instruction with an unrestricted slogan about freedom.
Connect liberty’s warning with the positive duty of loving service.
bke-tradition-christ
Test the Stated Contrast at Colossae

The warning names ways of being spoiled and concludes with a contrast involving Christ. Follow that actual contrast before importing an answer from a different part of the letter. Contextual reading begins with the sentence’s stated objects and direction.
Identify what the warning contrasts with Christ in this sentence.
bke-paul-wrested
Handle Difficult Writings Carefully

The passage acknowledges difficulty and warns about distortion of writings. Difficulty is not presented as permission to twist their meaning. The lesson is to take the warning seriously while distinguishing the named danger from an assumption that every difficult interpretation is already settled.
Recognize the warning against distorting difficult scriptural writings.
bke-assembly-seating
A Seat That Reveals Partiality

The two visitors are offered different treatment based on outward appearance. The narrative description is part of a criticism, not a seating policy to copy. Identifying who receives the preferred place helps expose the partiality being challenged.
Distinguish the described preference from conduct the passage approves.
bke-zion-law
Instruction Goes Forth from Zion

The vision connects peoples seeking instruction with law and the LORD’s word going forth. The place name matters within that movement toward learning and walking in his paths. Identifying the location does not require imposing a modern date on the vision.
Connect the named place with the vision’s movement toward instruction.
bke-kingdom-endures
The Kingdom That Stands

Daniel’s description contrasts the kingdom God establishes with kingdoms it consumes. Its endurance is explicitly stated rather than inferred from a contemporary political success. Keep the duration named in the interpretation distinct from proposed modern identifications.
Explain the stated endurance of the kingdom God establishes.
bke-wicked-return
Turning from Wickedness to Live

The contrast presents return from wicked ways as an alternative to death. Read the moral change named in the question, not merely the favourable outcome. The surrounding discussion concerns responsibility and repentance rather than permission to retain the wrongdoing.
Connect the offered life with the turning from wicked ways described.
bke-nations-tabernacles
Worship Among the Surviving Nations

The vision describes survivors coming year after year to worship the King and keep the named feast. The recurring action and the named participants matter alongside the feast’s identity. This description need not be given an unsupported modern timetable to be understood.
Identify the feast within the recurring worship described for the nations.
bke-stranger-welcomed
Care for the Stranger

The King’s description joins particular needs with concrete responses. Keep the response to a stranger distinct from the actions concerning food, drink or other needs. The lesson is attentive care as described in the scene, rather than an interchangeable list of benevolent words.
Identify the response matched to the stranger in the King’s description.
bke-tree-leaves
Leaves, Fruit and the Nations

John describes fruit and leaves with different associated details. Monthly fruit-bearing and the healing purpose of the leaves must not be interchanged. Careful observation of those separate descriptions supports a responsible reading before proposing a wider interpretation of the vision.
Distinguish the descriptions assigned to the tree’s fruit and leaves.
bke-rulers-answerable
Power and Accountable Counsel

The address to rulers links the source of power with examination of their works and counsels. Authority therefore appears alongside scrutiny. The lesson is not that receiving power establishes innocence, but that the passage places the powerful under examination.
Connect the source of authority with the scrutiny of rulers’ conduct.
bke-leader-covetousness
Qualifications Without Covetousness

The compared passages concern different responsibilities but share a moral qualification. Identify that overlap without equating every duty of an Israelite ruler and an overseer. Shared character language supports the comparison; it does not erase differences between their offices.
Recognize the shared qualification while preserving the offices’ distinct responsibilities.
bke-test-teaching
Receive, Examine and Retain the Good

The two passages join readiness to receive with examination and testing. Neither automatic acceptance nor reflexive rejection reproduces that combination. A teaching should be examined against Scripture, while the direction to retain good keeps testing from becoming mere suspicion.
Combine receptive hearing with examination and retaining what is good.
bke-gentle-correction
Restoration with Meekness

The compared instructions describe correction with meekness, and Galatians adds attention to the corrector’s own vulnerability. The aim and manner of restoration belong together. Being able to identify a fault does not remove the responsibility to correct without pride.
Connect restoration’s aim with meekness and self-watchfulness.
bke-testing-gold
The Image of Gold Tried by Fire

Both passages use testing imagery, while their immediate descriptions differ. Identify the image they share without assuming that every form of adversity has an identical explanation. The comparison invites attention to tested character or faith rather than a simplistic formula for every trial.
Recognize shared testing imagery while respecting the passages’ different contexts.
bke-asking-wisdom
Seek Wisdom from God

The passages describe prayer or asking followed by receiving understanding or wisdom. The shared direction is toward seeking from God. It is not the purchase of a title or the assumption that already possessing information removes the need to ask.
Recognize prayer and asking as the shared response in seeking wisdom.
Fringes That Recall Obedience

The instruction makes a visible feature serve remembrance and action. Looking at it is connected with remembering and doing the commandments rather than following one’s own heart and eyes. The object must not be separated from the responsibility it is given to recall.
Connect the commanded reminder with remembering and doing the commandments.
The Sabbath as Covenant Sign

The passage names Israel, continuing generations and the creation pattern. Keep those textual features together when describing the sign. Its covenant language should not be replaced with a claim that the observance is merely a personal preference without any stated relationship.
Recognize the recipients and creation-grounded sign language in the passage.
Read Fulfilment in Its Surrounding Words

The denial of destruction is followed by statements about the law and about doing and teaching commandments. Those surrounding words belong to the reading of fulfilment. The lesson preserves the statements without pretending that a single word settles every later interpretive question.
Read the fulfilment statement together with its surrounding commandments language.
Doing Good on the Sabbath

The account places the saying in a challenge about healing and an accusation. Yeshua’s comparison with rescuing a sheep leads to the expressed lawfulness of doing good. Retain that moral conclusion within the specific dispute instead of treating it as an unrelated slogan.
Explain the stated conclusion about doing good in the healing dispute.
Recurring Worship in Isaiah’s Vision

The scene connects enduring creation imagery, the people’s continuance and recurring worship. Identify the recurring times the passage names without manufacturing a calendar for the whole prophetic future. Textual observation and a proposed chronology are different tasks.
Recognize the recurring worship described without adding a prophetic timetable.
The Commanded Garment Reminder

The verse specifies recipients, garment borders and a blue cord. Read those actual features rather than invent measurements or a list of modern garments. The question asks what is made, while the command’s details prevent reducing it to a vague decoration.
Identify the commanded feature while retaining its stated garment details.
Fringes on the Garment’s Quarters

The instruction ties the fringes to the four quarters of the covering garment. Keep the object and placement together. A term used in another translation may help describe it, but the answer must still match the location specified in this instruction.
Locate the fringes according to the garment instruction itself.
Grooming: Preserve the Stated Boundaries

The verse names restrictions concerning both the head and beard. Its wording must be taught without replacing it with an invented modern style list or numerical measurement. Accurate instruction begins by distinguishing what the text expressly prohibits from an added rule.
Distinguish the expressed grooming restrictions from invented additional requirements.
The Apparel Distinction in the Command

The passage names a distinction concerning male and female apparel or items and gives a moral evaluation. It does not supply an exhaustive inventory of modern clothing. Preserve its stated distinction without pretending that every contemporary garment has been individually named.
Identify the command’s distinction without adding a universal modern garment list.
Daniel’s Prayer Continues

Daniel knows the writing has been signed, yet continues his established prayer and thanksgiving with windows toward Jerusalem. This is a narrative of his conduct under the decree. A description of his practice should not silently become an invented universal rule for every circumstance.
Recognize Daniel’s continued practice within the account of the signed decree.
The Priorities of the Model Prayer

The prayer begins with the Father’s name, Kingdom and will before requests for daily bread and forgiveness. The sequence directs attention beyond immediate needs. Preserve those opening priorities while also retaining the later requests rather than treating them as competing prayers.
Identify the God-directed priorities that open the model prayer.
Foreigners Who Hold the Covenant

The promise names people joining the LORD, serving him, loving his name and holding his covenant. Acceptance at the holy mountain is described with those conditions. Neither disregard the named foreigners nor remove the covenant and Sabbath language accompanying their welcome.
Preserve both the named recipients and conditions of the promised welcome.
Leaving, Cleaving and One Flesh

The sentence joins a departure, a new attachment and the resulting one-flesh relationship. Those features belong together in its description of marriage. Later use of the passage should begin with these stated relationships rather than add restrictions not supplied by this verse.
Explain the relationships joined in the one-flesh statement.
The Stated Danger in the Marriage Restriction

The command addresses named nations and supplies a reason concerning being turned toward other gods. Keep the recipients and reason within that covenant setting. It must not be expanded into a modern racial classification or a marriage rule the passage has not stated.
Preserve the restriction’s named scope and its expressly stated reason.
Marriage and Tribal Inheritance

The passage addresses daughters holding inheritance and permits choice within a specified tribal family. Its stated concern is land remaining with the tribe. Treating the provision as a rule about every marriage would omit the inheritance condition that gives the case its scope.
Explain the inheritance purpose and bounded recipients of this marriage provision.
The Particular Remarriage Case

Follow the sequence of marriages and endings described before identifying the prohibition on return to the first husband. The sequence defines the case. A summary that prohibits every remarriage would be broader than the particular return the passage forbids.
Apply the stated prohibition to its actual sequence rather than all remarriages.
Why One Animal Fails Both Criteria

The passage acknowledges the divided hoof while denying that the swine chews the cud. The classification follows the combined criteria, not one visible feature alone. This illustrates why a correct application must retain every required condition in the law’s description.
Explain why meeting one criterion does not satisfy both required features.
Blood, Life and the Altar

The instruction relates blood to life and to the role assigned on the altar, then states a prohibition with named recipients. Preserve those explanations instead of substituting an unprovided modern theory. The text’s stated meaning is what supports the answer.
Connect the blood prohibition with the passage’s own life-and-atonement explanation.
Dietary Conduct in a Judgment Scene

The prophecy names particular conduct within a severe judgment description. Recognize what is explicitly condemned without omitting it because the scene is difficult. The described divine action is not a commission for private people to enact punishment against others today.
Identify the conduct named while preserving the prophecy’s divine agent of judgment.
